newsitem.title: NORWAY: EU, North Sea states try to save fish stocks.
newsitem.headline: EU, North Sea states try to save fish stocks.

text.p: EU commissioners and ministers of fisheries and environment of North Sea states agreed on Friday on a set of recommendations to save North Sea fish stocks threatened with collapse because of overfishing.

The two-day conference in the Norwegian west coast city of Bergen, the first joint meeting of North Sea fisheries and environment ministers, was hailed as a success by EU fisheries commissioner Emma Bonino and EU environment commissioner Ritt Bjerregaard.

But a dispute over the jurisdiction of North Sea states triggered by the combative Bonino at first threatened to derail the talks and the non-binding final declaration, or Statement of Conclusions, was criticised by environmentalists as inadequate for saving depleted fish stocks.

"Cod in the North Sea is facing imminent collapse," Greenpeace delegation leader Malcolm MacGarvin said. "While the ministers have agreed to review progress every couple of years, there is little of substance for them to review."
Bjerregard, a Dane, said however: "Now decisions have been taken and we will see what comes out of this. This is not just hot air. We have concrete goals."

The two commissioners and officials from about 10 countries agreed that fisheries practices now resulted in the exploitation of a number of important fisk stocks such as cod and mackerel beyond sustainable levels.
They agreed to take a so-called precautionary approach in that the abense of sufficient scientific knowledge should not be used as a reason for postponing or failing to take conservation measures.

They invited competent authorities to suspend or reduce harvesting of depleted stocks, reduce fishing fleets and to take measures, if appropriate, to protect dense aggregations of spawning fish from excessive levels of exploitation. Total Allowable Catches (TAC) would be extended to stocks not covered by TAC.
Delegates said the use of the word "invited" was crucial and replaced a proposal which said ministers and commissioners "requested" that competent authorities follow up the recommendations.
Bonino, an Italian, said the European Union, not North Sea states, had formal jurisdiction over North Sea fishing.

"I have nothing against the political agreement. I am in favour of the contents. The problem for me was a legal one in the sense that the EU is made up of 15 states and the fisheries policies are common fisheries policies," she said.
Not only environmentalists but some delegations, including non-EU member Norway, had sought more drastic steps to protect the North Sea marine ecosystem and ensuring sustainable fisheries.

"Expectations were high but for natural reasons they could not all be fulfilled here in Bergen," said Erhard Jauck, German state secretary at the federal environment ministry. "To us the decisive progress made in Bergen is the knowledge that it is necessary to integrate fisheries policies with environmental policies."
